zh: 约束只涉及相邻两部电影：不能连续跳过两部。所以处理到某一部时，只需要知道上一部是选了还是跳了。
设 take 为当前这部被选时的最优和，skip 为当前这部被跳过时的最优和。选当前部可以接在任何合法状态之后；跳过当前部则上一部必须被选。
初始 take=0（空前缀可以继续）、skip=负无穷；对每个评分 x，同时更新 newTake=max(take,skip)+x、newSkip=take；最后输出 max(take,skip)。这样 n=1 时可以跳过唯一一部得到 0，n≥2 时自然不会全部跳过；和的绝对值不超过 10^8。
en: The constraint only involves neighbours: two consecutive movies cannot both be skipped. So at each movie you only need to know whether the previous one was taken or skipped.

Let take be the best sum when the current movie is chosen and skip the best sum when it is skipped. Choosing the current movie can follow any valid state; skipping it requires the previous movie to be chosen.

Start with take = 0 (the empty prefix can continue) and skip = negative infinity; for each rating x update simultaneously newTake = max(take, skip) + x and newSkip = take; print max(take, skip) at the end. With n = 1 this allows skipping the only movie for 0, and with n >= 2 it never skips everything; sums stay within 10^8 in absolute value.

explanationEn:
## Fixed original text and correction of a wrong explanation

The file fastprep/Akuna Capital/akuna-maximize-ratings.md at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc specifies: choose a subsequence of movies in their original order to maximize the sum of ratings, and you cannot skip two or more consecutive movies. The full range is 1 <= n <= 100000 and -1000 <= ratings[i] <= 1000, including 0. The original's internal example [-1, -3, -2] explicitly allows choosing only the second item, and also allows choosing the first and third; both are optimal at -3, which shows that skipping one movie at the start and one at the end are both allowed.

The original has no extra condition that the choice must be non-empty, and this problem does not add one: with n = 1, skipping the only movie is not skipping two consecutive movies, so the optimum for a single negative rating is 0. With n >= 2 it is impossible to skip everything, because at least two adjacent movies would be skipped. The empty choice has sum 0; this only affects edge cases such as a single non-positive rating, and does not mean an all-negative array can be skipped entirely.

Both original official outputs are kept: [-3, 2, 4, -1, -2, -5] chooses [2, 4, -2] for 4; [9, -1, -3, 4, 5] chooses [9, -1, 4, 5] for 17. The second original explanation omitted -1 and claimed 9 + 4 + 5 = 17, which is both an arithmetic error (it is actually 18) and a violation of the explicit definition, since it skips -1 and -3 consecutively; this site explicitly adds -1 back without changing the original output 17. The third public example, a single -1000 giving 0, is added by this site. stdin gives n and n ratings, and the output is one integer; no upstream code was executed.

## Approach

After processing a prefix, keep two optimal values: take, where the last movie is chosen, and skip, where the last movie is skipped. If the current rating x is chosen, it can follow any previous valid state, newTake = max(take, skip) + x; if it is skipped, the previous movie must have been chosen, so newSkip = take. Initialize take = 0 as a starting point from which the empty prefix can continue, and skip as negative infinity; after the first movie the two states naturally become x and 0. At the end take the maximum of the two.

## Proof of correctness

By induction, assume take and skip are the best sums over all valid plans of the prefix with the corresponding state of the last movie. Choosing the current movie never creates a new consecutive skip, so any old valid plan can be extended by x, and taking the maximum of the two old states gives the optimum over all plans that choose the current movie. When skipping the current movie, an old plan whose last movie was also skipped would be invalid, so the transition can only come from the old take; extending its best plan gives the optimum over all valid plans that skip the current movie. These two sets cover the valid plans of the new prefix without overlap or omission, so the update preserves the definitions.

The initialization lets the first movie be either chosen or skipped on its own, matching the rule for the start. There is no requirement to choose the last movie, so the maximum of the two final states is the best rating sum over all valid subsequences.

## Complexity and edge cases

Each movie updates only two numbers: time O(n), extra algorithm space O(1), and O(n) for reading the array. Every valid sum has absolute value at most 1000n <= 10^8, so an ordinary signed 32-bit integer can hold the final value; an implementation may use 64-bit or Python integers with a sufficiently small unreachable sentinel. All positive means choosing everything; all negative must still respect the no-two-adjacent-skips rule, so you cannot simply add the positive values. With n equal values of -1000, at least floor(n/2) movies are chosen and the result is -1000 * floor(n/2); a single negative movie gives 0.

## Independent verification

The small oracle enumerates every selection mask, rejects plans with any pair of adjacent unchosen positions, sums the kept ratings directly and takes the maximum, without using the reference state transition. All 163 unique oracle inputs run the actual reference subprocess; in addition, all 3279 arrays of length 1..7 with ratings -1/0/1 are enumerated exhaustively.

The large-domain independent algorithm starts from the sum of choosing everything and considers the cost saved by skipping negative ratings. An optimal plan never needs to skip a positive rating; skipping a 0 does not improve the value either, so those skips can be removed. Skipping index i is represented by the weighted interval [i, i+2) with weight -ratings[i], and two intervals not overlapping corresponds exactly to the two skipped positions not being adjacent. So weighted interval scheduling applies: sort by right end, binary search the previous compatible interval, get the maximum saving, and add it to the choose-everything sum. For example, for [-5] the choose-everything sum -5 plus the saving 5 gives 0. It does not call the reference take/skip states; it is cross-checked against the masks on the small domain first, generates the expected outputs on the large domain, and all-equal and alternating data get additional closed-form checks.

The official data covers the original examples, single positive/negative/zero movies, all negative, adjacent positives, skippable first and last movies, skipping every other movie, zero values, the extremes ±1000, and several complete structures of length 100000. The negative controls allow consecutive skips or force choosing the last movie; a wrong solution only counts as killed when it exits normally on every official input.
